Usually people refer to America's religious right as purely vengeful and while this is true in many cases, forgiveness and repentance are also pillars of the Christian faith. This manifests itself in several ways. You generally see it in the difference in sentencing by juries that think the "guilty" have shown true remorse. I would like to suggest the following, possibly controversial idea--that the belief in pure evil (BPE) begins with a belief that there is pure evil in oneself. That one responds to this by disowning (or attempting to disown) this part by what has been traditionally referred to as defense mechanisms, one of which is called projection--the idea that the evil is really in other people or a particular other person. That other then must be wiped out.

How one gets to feel evil inside oneself is probably by being so taught when young. Or by being blamed when very young--before one has a clear boundary between self and other. One experiences impulses which are hard to control (because one is young, say) or that one doesn't wish to control, and then powerful "caretakers" get angry at you. And so on.

Thanks for the interesting ama bud. I grew up in a small town with a kid whose father made the stuff illegally I believe as they made sure to keep it hush hush so my first question is what is the legality of what you do? Are there dangers involved and if so what are they, I mean in the actual process of brewing? Third what is the strongest alcohol you have made and what were its effects on you?

The moonshine tradition is a long and beautiful one. As long as there have been rat bastards trying to push people around, there have been those who have fought back and set up their stills against the law.

First, distilling in the United States is heavily regulated and even owning the equipment can lead to a visit from the feds.

The company I work for just started. We're a small group making a very unique craft spirit from maple syrup. The end result is a beverage that's somewhere between a rum and a bourbon. I might be biased, but I love it. If I'm not going to have an expensive scotch, I make a spirit that I enjoy every day.

The hardest part was going through the regulatory process. After prohibition, the remaining companies lobbied congress hard to create an environment where new companies would have a tough time setting up shop. If you want to set up a distillery, you better have a good lawyer, plenty of money, and be willing to wait for a long time.

The actual process is pretty simple. You take a fermented liquid (call the "wash") and run it through a still. Because alcohol has a different boiling point then water, a still can separate the alcohol from the rest of the fermented liquid.

Is it dangerous? Yup. Very. As the still first starts running, what comes off (the "foreshot") is a dangerous chemical that would poison you quick. You also have to worry about chemical compounds building up in the still. Unlike many distillers, we clean our still every morning before operation.

As we get into the middle of the run, what comes off is an alcohol that's between 160-180 proof. It's enough to make even a saesoned drinker's eyes bug out!
Thanks man, great reply! So does the alcohol taste like maple syrup? Are you using real, quality maple syrup and what made you guys decide to use maple syrup as a base?

No maple flavor. Instead it imparts some subtle notes. A hint of vanilla. A taste of nuttiness. Although similar to an oak aged rum, by using maple sugar instead of cane sugar or molasses, it makes it very different then anything you've ever tasted.

We wanted to make a unique beverage that utilized locally sourced product from New York State. We have an abundance of maple trees. It's expensive, but we purchase tons of the good stuff on a regular basis!
yeah that does sound tasty, don't suppose you would share the brand name? Where's it available?

As long as your mash isn't super pulpy, I wouldn't worry about the methanol in the heads so much as some less than tasty chemicals that fly off early.

It's too bad about the whole blindness thing, I work with pure methanol a lot as a chemist, and I always though that it smells like it would taste delicious.

I guess it depends on the definition of heads. I consider them separate from the foreshot, but some people don't when they're talking about them (although the idea of fortifying your wash with acetone, methanol, and other volitiles makes me queasy. Just throw out the foreshot!)
How do you tell when the heads end and the main batch has started? Also, how do you tell the tails from the main batch?

Excellent question.

For those who don't know, the art of distilling comes from making "cuts", or separating the running based on a number of factors. Generally speaking, a run is divided into three stages. The "heads", the "hearts" and the "tails". The hearts are the good part. It's what you want. The tails are weaker, but can be run through again to generate more hearts, and the heads are only good for fortifying the wash.

We have a couple of methods. Obviously, smell is a big factor, as well as shaking the running to observe the bubbles. We also take numerous samples throughout the run, proof them, and then chart every sample into a database. We have the numbers pretty much dialed in, but it's still a work in progress.

The most important method is taste. The silver of the hearts tastes so amazingly good, there's no mistaking it!
I heard that if you don't do it right that you could go blind? Is this true or just and old wives tale?

Sadly, this is partly true. One of the compounds that is generated in the process is methyl alcohol. If you were to drink this, it could cause significant damage, including blindness. The thing is, when it comes off the still there's no mistaking it. You wouldn't want to drink it. Even giving it a whiff is enough to put you off.

The other danger comes from some of the materials the moonshiners used to use. Lead is, obviously, cheaper and easier to work with then copper...but that meant significant lead and other chemicals in the final product. Really, really bad for you. (Even copper needs to be cleaned religiously!)

How much do you have invested in this endeavor? Many years ago, I looked into starting my own distilling business and found out that state laws made it so prohibitively expensive that it wouldn't be worth it. I think I had it figured that licensing, buying a plot of land not attached or adjacent to a residential area, building a building up to state code for the production of alcohol, etc., was going to cost me well over $150k before I could even legally produce my first drop.

I always had a feeling that most of these costs were to ensure that the "big boys" didn't have any competition.

Nice thing for me is that I'm an employee, not an owner. Actually, the only employee. Chiefs outnumber the Indians by a 3-1 margin. I only bring my knowledge and expertise to the table. I get to do all the fun stuff, and leave the headaches to others. After working for myself the past five years, this is the most enjoyable change of pace I could imagine.

I don't want to betray any confidences here, but I would say that going into the business is going to be about as expensive as you think. That's a pretty good number, actually. The liquor industry is like beer. It's the economy of scale. You could probably start with a single small still and a few barrels, but you won't realize a profit like that for a very, very, very long time.

You're also correct that the game is rigged. The regulations that exist act as a gigantic barrier to entry. I suspect that this is viewed by some as a feature, not a bug.

Now, all that being said, I think it's an incredible market to be jumping into. It's like getting into gourmet coffee in the late eighties, or craft brewing in the late nineties. Craft spirits are going to be this decades big change. Just like it's hard to imagine going back to a world with only a few crappy beers to choose from, in fifteen years we'll be amazed by how crappy our liquor options were. Getting into now is the right time. (Of course, having lost investors for my brewery, such things are easier said than done.)

What many are neglecting to realize is that we live in a culture of convenience. This site is not convenient. Sure, the site will continue to grow, but it will do so at a much lower rate than it otherwise could have. When arbitrary limits and barriers are set, they only serve to hinder new users from joining and using the site regularly as so much effort is required just to get started.

Instead of driving new users away with limits on participation, the site and its features should be designed in such a way as to allow and encourage new users to join and participate however they see fit. I understand the desire to have the user base directly participate by commenting and discussing with others but any website you check you will find that the majority of users are simply consumers. Whether this be blogs, forums, video sharing websites, or any others, most people go to partake of the content and not to actively comment or share as that takes more time and effort.

The majority of Internet users do not wish to expand any more time and effort than is necessary to get there fix of media or information consumption and by requiring greater amounts of time and effort from potential users this serves to encourage them to use competitors such as Reddit that conveniently provide the basic features they desire.

This is not say that the problems these limits are meant to address do not exist, simply that those problems should be addressed in a different way. Does the vote cap really need to be so low? Why do only up votes one receives to their comments count and not up votes received for submitted content? Why is there a restriction on how much content can be submitted? For instance, after submitting six links last night I have been blocked from submitting any further ones for no reason I can discern. This is a fairly new site that is sorely lacking on content and I wished to do what I could to expand that but have been blocked from doing so. This only serves to slow the pace which the site can grow.

I think everyone that is saying to just comment are falling prey to a few fallacies. One could be that they had to go through this somehow everyone else has to as a form of initiation. A second, they are already past the hurdle and have lost perspective of the annoyance that a new user would feel and how this could turn them away. A third, they could simply have gotten used to the idea and see the issues these things are meant to address and simply buckled down on these being the only solutions instead of trying to come up with more elegant solutions that do not stifle growth. They take the if it ain't broke don't fix it mindset instead of the if it ain't broke make it better mindset.

A transaction may be safely sent without fees if these conditions are met:

  • It is smaller than 1,000 bytes.
  • All outputs are 0.01 BTC or larger.
  • Its priority is large enough (see the Technical Info section below)

Otherwise, the reference implementation will round up the transaction size to the next thousand bytes and add a fee of 0.1 mBTC (0.0001 BTC) per thousand bytes. As an example, a fee of 0.1 mBTC (0.0001 BTC) would be added to a 746 byte transaction, and a fee of 0.2 mBTC (0.0002 BTC) would be added to a 1001 byte transaction. Users may increase the default 0.0001 BTC/kB fee setting, but cannot control transaction fees for each transaction. Bitcoin-Qt does prompt the user to accept the fee before the transaction is sent (they may cancel the transaction if they are not willing to pay the fee).

Note that a typical transaction is 500 bytes, so the typical transaction fee for low-priority transactions is 0.1 mBTC (0.0001 BTC), regardless of the number of bitcoins sent.
